newsitem.title: HUNGARY: CHIRAC SAYS RUSSIA TRIP ON DESPITE YELTSIN ILLNESS.
newsitem.headline: CHIRAC SAYS RUSSIA TRIP ON DESPITE YELTSIN ILLNESS.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Friday his forthcoming trip to Russia in early February was still on despite Russian President Boris Yeltsin's health problems.
"For the moment the date has not been put in doubt," Chirac told reporters on the second day of a two-day state visit to Hungary.

Moscow announced earlier this week that Chirac would visit Russia on February 2. Yeltsin was admitted to hospital last week with pneumonia only weeks after leaving hospital following a quintuple by-pass heart operation.
Kremlin officials on Thursday said Yeltsin's health had "stabilised significantly".
Chirac was speaking at a joint press conference following talks with Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn which centred on the enlargement of both the European Union (EU) and NATO.
Chirac warned that the enlargement of NATO must be well prepared in advance with full consultation with all sides and with due regard for Russia's sensitivities.
"(The enlargement) must be done in a way which does not give Russia the sentiment of being humiliated or confronted," he said.
Horn stressed Hungary's right to make its own decisions over NATO.
"The question of our membership of NATO is a sovereign matter," he said. "We alone must define our security interests."
Chirac said he stood by the forecast he made on Thursday that the first wave of admissions to the EU, including that of Hungary, should take place by 2000.

"I do not wish to have raised false hopes -- we need ambitions and the will, if we have the will there is a chance we will succeed," he said, adding that target date was shared by Chancellor Helmut Kohl of Germany.

Earlier Chirac, addressing a gathering of industrialists, praised Hungary for honouring its debts left by communism, describing the country as a reliable long-term trading partner which "honoured its word and its signature".
But he appealed to Hungary to increase its trade with France.
"There seem to be no large deals with Hungary," he said. "I can understand we are not always the best but I fail to see that we are always the least good," he said.
"That would be a real Hungarian exception."

A dozen top French industrialists are accompanying the president, including the chairmen of state electricity and gas companies EDF and GDF, missiles and electronics firm Matra, and construction giant Bouygues.

EDF and GDF have bought stakes worth up to $400 million in Hungary's energy distribution network while Bouygues has a 35 percent stake in the company which built a new stretch of Hungary's southern motorway.
Chirac said such large investments have made France Hungary's third largest investor but she remained only its fifth largest trading partner.
"This can be improved still further," he said.
